brief: Oil's jump reignited a broader bond selloff. Brent rose to $106.60, having hit $108.16 intraday, on Iranian escalation warnings and a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia, pushing the 10yr Treasury yield to a post-2007 high of 5.20% and the 30yr to 5.48%, the biggest 2-day 10yr rise since last spring's Liberation Day turmoil. The author's central point is that the selloff is driven almost entirely by real yields (+9.8bps to a post-2008 high of 2.87%), not breakevens (-1.3bps), so markets show no added longer-term inflation concern despite oil up around 75% in 2026, and a term premium range bound for 18 months argues the move isn't fiscal. The author's own view is that breakevens look too low and real yields may be getting too high. Reuters reported the US and Iran are exploring a phased Strait of Hormuz reopening deal, briefly pulling Brent down $4, though Iran's competing 7-day ceasefire proposal stays tied to a June MoU the US has resisted. Resilient US data, including jobless claims and new home sales, plus a strong German Ifo reading, added to the hawkish pressure. S&P 500 breadth was negative but Mag-7 gains limited the index's decline.
